title: Cabinet approves Rs 3,230 crore plan to turn North and South Block into the Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum
dek: The approval on 11 November gives the museum a budget and a timetable: implementation in phases to 2030-31, with a first gallery, on adornment, due to open in North Block in the latter part of 2027.
body: The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by the Prime Minister, approved the development of the Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum at the North and South Block complex in New Delhi on Wednesday 11 November 2026. The estimated cost is Rs 3,230 crore, as appraised by the Public Investment Board on 27 July 2026, according to the government's statement as carried by the news agencies and DD News.

The museum will reuse the historic North and South Block buildings, following the relocation of government offices, and the government says their architectural character will be kept. The proposed built-up area is about 1,78,509 square metres. The government describes it as the museum with the largest display area in the world, measured against major international museums.

Work is to be carried out in phases between 2026-27 and 2030-31. The first gallery, on the theme of adornment, is expected to open to the public in North Block in the latter part of 2027, and further galleries are to be added in modules over time. Themes named so far include Architecture and Cityscapes, Mathematics and Astronomy, Languages and Scripts, Faith and Spirituality, and Bharat Connects, on trade and ideas.

According to the government, around 1.8 million objects have been identified for the museum from the National Museum and other Ministry of Culture museums, 52 site museums of the Archaeological Survey of India, state museums and private collections. The statement also says the museum is being equipped to handle one crore (ten million) visitors a year.

The Prime Minister first announced the museum on 18 May 2023. The statement says the content and collection analysis is still being done, and it does not say what will happen to the present National Museum building on Janpath.
